title: SMSF curbs 'will shake confidence across spectrum'
full_text:
Australia's new housing pipeline will lose an expected 2500 homes from self-managed super funds that pulled out of signed contracts they could have continued despite the federal Labor government's budget changes, the Housing Industry Association said on Monday.
The HIA, which made the prediction based on feedback from its home-builder members, said the effective ban on SMSFs borrowing to invest in residential property that came into effect on Monday would further hold back national cabinet's already-challenged 1.2 million home target.
"The principal reason is buyers have a loss of confidence," HIA chief economist Tim Reardon said. "The buyers are choosing to walk away from their signed contracts rather than bear the risk of future policy changes."
The measure that the government in June said would affect only 4000 loans a year - a total the industry said vastly underestimated both the volume of loans and their strategic importance in providing early sales that developers needed to unlock construction finance - would shake buyers across both new home building and residential sales, industry figures said.
"Confidence across the spectrum in the Australian housing market has been shattered over the course of the last 12 months," said Real Estate Institute of Australia president Jacob Caine.
"Obviously, we have the global political and macroeconomic factors contributing to this lack of confidence but the significance and boldness of the regulatory and taxation changes that have occurred prove that the course of the last few months has completely undermined the confidence that developers, sellers, buyers and renters have in our incredibly fragile housing system."
Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg will this week propose an amendment to the rules, hoping to reverse the restriction on SMSF borrowing.
Housing is not the only sector affected. The new rules do not ban SMSFs from borrowing to invest in residential property as such, but rather limit the scope of permitted borrowing to "business real property", meaning land used wholly and exclusively in one or more businesses.
This would also prevent many SMSFs from investing in commercial property assets that had dual use by including both residential and commercial use in one site, said Rasti Vaibhav, the head of buyers' agency Get RARE Properties.
This would be a particular problem in regional areas, Vaibhav said. "Doctors, pharmacists, vets, motels and roadhouses often trade from mixed-use premises that will not qualify. The test is 'business real property', not 'commercial', and it turns on use, not zoning."
One consequence of the change was that SMSF investors wanting to borrow to buy commercial property would all focus on smaller-scale assets that were clearly only used for business purposes, and which sat in a $500,000-to-$1.2 million price range, Vaibhav said.
The most common price point of residential asset that an SMSF investor would now be looking to apply to commercial property would be in the $600,000-to-$700,000 range, he said.
Likely investments could be metro area office or retail properties and small industrial warehouses. The volume of SMSF investors in commercial assets was not large enough to shift the market significantly, but it would inflate prices, Vaibhav said.
The Australian Taxation Office confirmed the new rules. "Limited recourse borrowing arrangements [LRBAs] are not banned," a spokesperson said. "SMSFs can still borrow or maintain a borrowing under an LRBA to acquire an asset. However, the changes restrict real property assets to business real property."
Not all mixed-use property was automatically excluded. "Rather, the relevant question is whether the property is used wholly and exclusively in one or more businesses. In applying that test, the significance of any non-business use must be considered in the context of the arrangement."
